The **employees.csv** file is **not clean enough** for a reliable salary analysis. ### What the quality check revealed | Issue | Details | |-------|---------| | **Missing values** | • Department: 2 rows
• Age: 2 rows
• Salary: 3 rows **(critical for salary analysis)**
• Start date: 1 row
• Email: 2 rows | | **Duplicate employee IDs** | • ID 6 – appears 2 times (exact duplicate)
• ID 8 – appears 2 times (conflicting data)
• ID 12 – appears 2 times (exact duplicate) | | **Total rows** | 23 rows (including the duplicates) | ### Why this matters for salary analysis 1. **Missing salary values** – 3 records lack a salary, so any aggregate (average, median, total) would be biased unless those rows are handled (e.g., imputed or removed). 2. **Duplicate IDs** – Duplicate records can double‑count employees or introduce conflicting information (as with ID 8), which would distort any per‑employee calculations. 3. **Other missing fields** – While not directly about salary, missing department, age, etc., can affect grouping or stratified analyses (e.g., salary by department or age group). ### Recommendation Before proceeding with salary analysis you should: 1. **Resolve duplicates** – Decide whether to keep the first occurrence, merge the conflicting data, or remove one of the copies. 2. **Handle missing salaries** – Either remove those rows or impute reasonable values after investigating why they are missing. 3. **Address other missing fields** – Fill or remove rows with missing department/age/start_date/email if those attributes are needed for further breakdowns. Only after these cleaning steps can you trust the salary statistics derived from this dataset.
